source.title: Scaling Experiments in Self-Supervised Cross-Table Representation Learning
source.authors: Maximilian Schambach; D. Paul; J. Otterbach

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some appendix dataset text is garbled, but that does not prevent reading the relevant scaling results.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size and training duration and evaluates held-out downstream performance, but uses self-supervised tabular pretraining and linear-probe metrics rather than the original double-descent setup.
record.gate_note: The main scaling results evaluate linear-probe performance on benchmark evaluation splits. Appendix B mentions a double-descent-like single-table training loss, but that is a training loss, not test error, so it is not recorded as a result row. Training imputation accuracy and loss are likewise not rows for the test-error claims.
record.test_reason: This is a scaling study of a self-supervised tabular Transformer. It does not test double descent. Its size sweep has only three backbone sizes per setting (S/M/L or M/L/XL), and no interpolation threshold is identified. The measure is linear-probe performance on frozen self-supervised representations, not test error of a model fit to the training labels. Checkpoints are indexed by pretraining tokens on a masked-imputation objective, not by epochs of supervised training. None of these setups can show or rule out a fall-rise-fall curve around interpolation. Double descent appears only in a passing appendix remark: single-table training loss looks 'double-descent-like', cited to Nakkiran et al. The authors call it speculative and have no validation set to check it.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors report generally higher linear-probe performance at larger scale, saturation in single-table models, and only slight cross-table gains likely limited by data or compute. They also note that longer cross-table pretraining brought no systematic downstream gains. They make no claim about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a new Transformer architecture for self-supervised cross-table tabular pretraining, varies model scale and training duration, and evaluates held-out downstream linear-probe metrics. It does not reproduce the original double-descent experiments or identify an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and pretraining setup (single-table versus cross-table) change the reported scaling behavior; in cross-table experiments, updating versus freezing the backbone also affects performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear-probe performance of self-supervised tabular representations rises slightly with backbone size and saturates at M for smaller datasets. In the cross-table setting it shows no strong size trend, with some worse instances (e.g. California Housing). Performance shows no systematic change across pretraining checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling behaviour of self-supervised tabular Transformers under linear probing (not a double-descent claim).

fits_no_version.finding: Single-table training loss on HELOC and California Housing with the L model is described as 'double-descent-like' (Appendix B, Fig. 6). It is a training loss with no validation set, and the authors call its interpretation speculative.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-loss curve shape in self-supervised tabular pretraining.

record.problems: The benchmark evaluation uses five datasets and the paper reports no hyperparameter optimization. The scaling curves are presented in figures without stated numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The downstream metric is linear-probe performance, not a direct test-error sweep around an interpolation threshold.

untested.parts: All of V1. No supervised test-error sweep across model size around an interpolation threshold.
All of V2. No epoch-indexed supervised test error.
All of V3. Sample size is not swept.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' classification and its challenges/limits_scope labels for V1 and V2 should be dropped. The absence of a fall-rise-fall curve here is uninformative: there are only three model sizes, no interpolation threshold, a linear-probe measure, and a self-supervised token-checkpoint axis. The only mention of double descent concerns a training-loss curve, which the authors themselves treat as speculative.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not locate a peak relative to the model size that just fits the training set; its evaluation is downstream linear probing of self-supervised tabular representations.
Training progress is measured by processed tokens and checkpointed models, not explicitly by epochs; the study does not test whether any peak is near an interpolation threshold.
Training sample size is not swept to measure whether more data raises test error near an interpolation threshold.
The study evaluates one proposed architecture family, not double descent across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak locations across axes.
The study does not test label-noise or regularization dependence, multiple descent peaks, or disappearance of a peak under tuned regularization.
The study does not recast model complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that changes the curve to an ordinary U-shape.

relation.reason: Appendix B discusses double-descent-like training loss and speculative interpolation or grokking, but provides no corresponding validation-loss measurement.

tranche.reason: The study measures representation quality across model sizes and pretraining checkpoints without establishing a double-descent generalization curve or interpolation threshold.

source_check.notes: The pack's assertion that the authors make no double-descent claim overlooks Appendix B's training-loss observation, which does not establish any claim version. Single-table S/M/L training budgets also differ: 5 M, 10 M, and 25 M sampled rows.
